aspects.says: Index ranges over one array avoid the allocation of copying subarrays.
aspects.reason: a performance claim no test can observe deterministically; sum-task and min-max already work on index ranges

aspects.says: Without a threshold check the recursion never stops.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: every RecursiveTask practice on this page needs its base case to finish at all, and the split-tree practice of page 6.6.1.4 has an edge on a split that must always make progress

aspects.says: cancel(true) on a ForkJoinTask does not interrupt a task that is already running, and a failed subtask does not cancel its sibling.
RecursiveTask, RecursiveAction and CountedCompleter all extend ForkJoinTask, which implements Future.
aspects.reason: background taxonomy with nothing to practise; the practices use RecursiveTask and the Future methods directly

aspects.says: Each task returns its own result and the parent combines them at the join, instead of writing into shared mutable state.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: a solution that writes into a synchronized shared holder returns the same answers, so no test can tell it from one that combines results at the join; min-max follows the page's pure pattern

aspects.says: Computing one subtask with compute() instead of forking it keeps the current thread busy while the forked half runs elsewhere.
aspects.reason: forking both halves also runs them together, so no deterministic test can tell a solution that computes one half inline from one that forks both; the cost of the extra fork is asked in the overview page's quiz

aspects.says: compute() solves a range of at most threshold elements sequentially and otherwise splits it and runs the two halves at the same time.
A recursive Fibonacci task needs a sequential cutoff, because naive recursion creates an exponential number of tasks.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: get() on a failed task wraps the failure in an ExecutionException.
aspects.reason: practised by the within practice of page 6.6.1.1, whose failed task is reported through get()'s ExecutionException

aspects.says: join() and invoke() rethrow a subtask's RuntimeException unwrapped, possibly as a copy made in another thread whose cause is the original.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: Sums of large int arrays are kept in a long so they do not overflow.
A merge-sort RecursiveTask returns a new sorted array, merging the two sorted halves it joined.
A max or min search starts from Integer.MIN_VALUE or Integer.MAX_VALUE so negative numbers are handled.
RecursiveTask is a poor fit for I/O-bound, tiny, interdependent or order-dependent work.
aspects.reason: a judgement about when to choose the tool, not code a test can grade; blocking inside a pool is practised by the managed-block practice of page 6.6.1.1

aspects.says: RecursiveTask is Serializable but meant for in-process parallelism.
aspects.reason: incidental detail the page itself calls rarely useful, not practised

aspects.says: A midpoint split of N elements with threshold T makes a tree of depth about log2(N/T), with about 2^d leaves and 2^(d+1) - 1 tasks.
aspects.reason: practised by the split-tree practice of page 6.6.1.4, which counts the depth, leaves and tasks of a split for any split point

aspects.says: Invalid input such as an empty range for a max is refused early, in the task's constructor.
